column2: Type the company’s ticker or name into Codal’s search and pick it from the list. Watch out for similar tickers, such as rights, which have an “H” at the end.
Advanced search lets you choose the report type and date range.
Take the numbers from the Excel version or the web table; take the explanations and the auditor’s opinion from the PDF.
A “correction” means the earlier version had a mistake. If a company issues many corrections, its reports are careless.
Like looking for a book in a library: you search for its name, but you have to make sure you picked the right edition and author.
Monthly report: comes about 10 days after each month and is the earliest news on sales.
3, 6 and 9-month reports: profit and loss for several months. Annual report: complete and audited, before the meeting.
Interpretive report: managers explain what happened and what they plan.
Urgent announcements are important news, and the annual meeting approves the dividend.
Like a school report card: monthly marks arrive early, but the end-of-year report card is more complete and official.
Types of report, in simple words
From the money from sales, subtract the cost of making the product: that’s gross profit.
Subtract admin and selling costs too: that’s operating profit, the profit from the company’s main work. This is the most important number.
Then loan interest, side income and tax are counted, and net profit is what’s left.
“Other income” is usually one-off gains, like selling a piece of land; it won’t repeat.

A sandwich shop: sales for the month 100, bread and meat 60 (gross profit 40), rent and wages 25 (operating profit 15). If this month it also sold its old fridge for 5, that 5 isn’t from the main work.
The balance sheet is a snapshot of the company’s assets and debts on one day.
Inventory and money owed by customers; bank loans; “advances received” means customers paid in advance, a sign of good demand.
Retained earnings: profit that wasn’t paid out and stayed in the company.
Assets under construction: projects whose building isn’t finished yet.
Like counting your family’s assets: the house, the car, money in the bank, what relatives owe you, minus the instalments still to pay.
The cash flow statement says how much cash really came in and went out.
If a company shows high profit for years but less cash comes from its work, its profit is stuck in customer debts or the warehouse.
The statement of changes in equity shows how capital and retained earnings changed.
“Revaluation surplus” is just an accounting number, not money.
A shop that sells everything on credit has big sales on paper, but at the end of the month it has no money for the rent.
The auditor is an independent accountant who checks the reports are correct and writes an opinion.
“Unqualified”: no important problems. “Qualified”: an important but limited problem; work out its effect.
“Adverse” means the report as a whole is misleading, and a “disclaimer” means the auditor didn’t get enough evidence. Set both aside.
Like an inspection before buying a car: “sound”, “a few small issues”, “serious paint and accident damage”, or “they didn’t let us look”. The last two mean don’t buy.
The auditor’s opinion, in simple words
In Iran most companies get a “qualified” report; so the word “qualified” itself isn’t a reason to panic.
Read each qualification: for example tax counted lower than it really is, or old debts not collected.
What matters is how big the problem is and what kind it is.
An inspector saying “there’s a scratch on the wing” is very different from “the chassis is damaged”; both are problems.
Iranian companies report under Iranian accounting standards; a few large companies also have an international (IFRS) version.
In Iran, numbers aren’t updated for inflation.
Companies sometimes revalue their assets and then do a capital increase, which brings in no new money.
There are two versions of a report: “parent” for the company itself and “consolidated” for the company and its subsidiaries.
Like two accounts: your personal account (parent), and the whole family’s account with the children (consolidated).
In a note in Bahman 1398, Dr. Khosravani listed these duties of a listed company (the rules may have changed):
Financial statements with the auditor’s opinion, on time. If it made a loss, give the reason and plan within 15 days. Report project progress every 6 months.
If the auditor gives an “adverse” opinion or a “disclaimer”, the ticker is halted.
If accumulated losses exceed half the capital and aren’t fixed within a year, the share is removed from the exchange board.
Like the rules of an apartment building: each unit must pay its charges on time and report; otherwise it’s fined.
